newsitem.title: USA: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS/IBM, Intel options again lead.
newsitem.headline: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS/IBM, Intel options again lead.

text.p: With shares of International Business Machines Corp and Intel Corp leading the stock market higher Monday, options on those stocks led broad options trading.
By about 1300 CST/1900 GMT, IBM was ahead 2-5/8 at 161-3/4, off its session high of 163-3/8. Intel was up one at 139-3/8 after reaching a new all-time high of 141-3/4.
Volume was heavy in both shares.
IBM options, both puts and calls, were the most actively traded on the Chicago Board Options Exchange, while Intel puts and calls were the most active on the American Stock Exchange.
Traders said there did not appear to be a preponderance of buying or selling, with strong two-way trading seen in calls and puts in both sets of options.
Michael Schwartz, managing director at Oppenheimer & Co, said much of the volume in the IBM 140 and 160 calls could be investors rolling positions to the higher strike price.
The January 140 call traded more than 6,900 contracts and the January 160 call traded about 5,350.
The busiest IBM option was the January 140 put, which traded nearly 7,300 contracts.
"They could be buying back the puts and rolling up the calls," Schwartz said.
IBM January 140 puts were down 1/8 at 1/8 and the January 140 calls rose three to 22-1/2. The January 160 calls added 1-1/8 to 4-5/8.
Few investors appeared to be rolling positions into longer-dated options, with the February, April and July series seeing relatively thin trade.
Intel call options snared the most trading, led by the January 140, which traded about 6,050 contracts. The January 135 call traded nearly 3,900 and the January 145 traded 3,345.

Some of the Intel options activity in the January series could be from investors buying ahead of the company's quarterly earnings report, which is likely to be released before the January expiration, said Robert Dickey, managing director at Dain Bosworth.
He said investors often buy the options ahead of earnings reports and then sell on their release.
Harrison Roth, a first vice president at Cowen & Co, said some of the most interesting Intel options activity was in the long-term options known as LEAPS.
